primary_text_note: In copyright. Verified against an archive.org scan of the 1929 printing (in.ernet.dli.2015.209119), grepped verbatim; a few pages are missing from the scan (Act 3 Sc 1 pre-raid), covered by LitCharts/GradeSaver.

findings.claim: Stanhope's line “It's the only way to forget.” Used as a set-piece quotation in L1 (content, practice Q3, flashcard), L5 (key fact, conclusion, flashcard) and L7 (exam tip, practice Q1 stimulus, knowledge-check match list, flashcard).
findings.truth: No such line exists in the play. The real line is Stanhope to Raleigh, Act 3 Scene 2: “To forget, you little fool — to forget! D'you understand? To forget!” For drinking specifically the real line is Act 1: “if I went up those steps into the front line — without being doped with whiskey — I'd go mad with fright.” Students were told to memorise a fabrication for a closed-book paper.
findings.evidence: archive.org scan of the 1929 Gollancz printing of Journey's End (in.ernet.dli.2015.209119), grepped verbatim; “forget” appears only at Act 3 Sc 2. LitCharts and GradeSaver quotation lists carry no such line.

findings.claim: “Raleigh whispers that it is getting dark, and Stanhope quietly says ‘It's just the light — it's nearly morning.’” Repeated as “His lie” in the collapsible and in two flashcards.
findings.truth: Fabricated. Raleigh says “Could we have a light? It's — it's so frightfully dark and cold.” Stanhope answers “Sure! I'll bring a candle and get another blanket,” leaves, and Raleigh dies alone while he is away. Stanhope's comforting untruths are that the wound has “just gone through a bit” and that Raleigh has “a Blighty one.”
findings.evidence: archive.org scan of the 1929 Gollancz printing of Journey's End (in.ernet.dli.2015.209119), grepped verbatim, Act 3 Scene 3 (final pages).

findings.claim: Key Fact: Stanhope tells Hibbert “If you went — and left Osborne and Trotter and Raleigh and all the other men who are staying here — I'd rather spare you than any of them.” The sentence then breaks mid-way (“…them.” threatens to shoot Hibbert…”).
findings.truth: Fabricated hybrid. Stanhope says: “If you went, I'd have you shot — for deserting. It's a hell of a disgrace — to die like that. I'd rather spare you the disgrace.” His admission is “Because I feel the same — exactly the same!”
findings.evidence: archive.org scan of the 1929 Gollancz printing of Journey's End (in.ernet.dli.2015.209119), grepped verbatim, Act 2 Scene 2.

findings.claim: “Raleigh's line ‘How awfully nice — if the Dosch didn't tell — and Dosch didn't know’ reveals his boyish excitement.” Also quoted in practice Q5.
findings.truth: Fabricated, and misattributed. “Dosch” is not a word in the play (Sherriff writes “Boche”). “How awfully nice — if the brigadier's pleased” is Stanhope's bitter line to the Colonel in Act 3 Scene 1, after Osborne's death. Raleigh's real Act 1 excitement is “I could have cheered” and “Dennis'll be frightfully surprised to see me.”
findings.evidence: archive.org scan of the 1929 Gollancz printing of Journey's End (in.ernet.dli.2015.209119), grepped verbatim, Act 1 and Act 3 Scene 1.

findings.claim: “The one man I could talk to as a friend” is presented as Raleigh's line about Stanhope — as an essay stimulus (L7 Q2), a 4-mark question (L5 Q5), a knowledge-check match option and a flashcard.
findings.truth: Wrong speaker, wrong subject and wrong wording. It is Stanhope, Act 3 Scene 2, about the dead Osborne: “The one man I could trust — my best friend — the one man I could talk to as man to man — who understood everything.”
findings.evidence: archive.org scan of the 1929 Gollancz printing of Journey's End (in.ernet.dli.2015.209119), grepped verbatim, Act 3 Scene 2.

findings.claim: Practice Q3 asks students to analyse “You think there's no limit to what a man can bear?” to reveal Stanhope's state of mind “in Act 1”, and the mark scheme says it is “directed at Osborne”.
findings.truth: The line is Act 3 Scene 2, shouted at Raleigh after Osborne's death. The lesson's own content_html says exactly this, so the question contradicted the article. Replaced with the genuine Act 1 line to Osborne about whisky.
findings.evidence: archive.org scan of the 1929 Gollancz printing of Journey's End (in.ernet.dli.2015.209119), grepped verbatim, Act 3 Scene 2.

findings.claim: Osborne “organises earwig races” (L5), “tells Raleigh about the earwig races” (L2), and “talks about earwig races hours before a raid” (L6 content, key fact, mark scheme, flashcard).
findings.truth: The earwig races are Hardy's. In Act 1 Hardy explains the rules to Osborne, says he won ten francs the night before, and advises dipping the earwig in whiskey. Osborne never runs one, and never mentions them to Raleigh.
findings.evidence: archive.org scan of the 1929 Gollancz printing of Journey's End (in.ernet.dli.2015.209119), grepped verbatim, Act 1 (Hardy–Osborne handover).

findings.claim: “Stanhope objects to sending Osborne on such a dangerous mission, but the Colonel insists” (L3 key fact, L3 content, L3 flashcard, L5 content, two mark schemes).
findings.truth: Stanhope's objection is to Raleigh, not Osborne: “He's awfully new to it all… It's rotten to send a fellow who's only just arrived.” He accepts the Colonel's choice of Osborne without argument.
findings.evidence: archive.org scan of the 1929 Gollancz printing of Journey's End (in.ernet.dli.2015.209119), grepped verbatim, Act 2 Scene 2 (Colonel–Stanhope).

findings.claim: Raleigh's letter “describes Stanhope as ‘the best company commander in the battalion’” (L3 content, L3 flashcard, L3 mark scheme); “the Colonel calls him ‘the best company commander in the battalion’” (L5); “Stanhope is called the best company commander in the battalion” (L7).
findings.truth: Two different lines have been merged. The letter says “Dennis is the finest officer in the battalion, and the men simply love him… I'm awfully proud to think he's my friend.” “He's a long way the best company commander we've got” is Osborne's defence of Stanhope to Hardy in Act 1. The Colonel never says it.
findings.evidence: archive.org scan of the 1929 Gollancz printing of Journey's End (in.ernet.dli.2015.209119), grepped verbatim, Act 1 and Act 2 Scene 1.

findings.claim: “The night before the raid, Osborne and Raleigh sit together in the dugout. Osborne reads aloud from Alice's Adventures in Wonderland… one or both may die tomorrow.” Repeated in a knowledge check stem and a flashcard.
findings.truth: Two separate moments. Osborne reads Alice in Act 2 Scene 2 and Trotter mocks him for reading “a kid's book”. The Osborne–Raleigh scene, where Osborne quotes the book aloud and they talk about home, is Act 3 Scene 1, minutes before the raid on the Wednesday afternoon — not the night before.
findings.evidence: archive.org scan of the 1929 Gollancz printing of Journey's End (in.ernet.dli.2015.209119), grepped verbatim Act 2 Sc 2; LitCharts Act 3 Scene 1 summary for the pre-raid scene (pages missing from the scan).

findings.claim: “He offers Osborne a box of cigars as a reward” (content, flashcard, mark scheme).
findings.truth: The Colonel offers Osborne nothing. Osborne himself reports that headquarters has laid on two bottles of champagne, six cigars and a fresh chicken for the celebration after the raid.
findings.evidence: LitCharts Act 3 Scene 1 summary; the Colonel–Stanhope raid conversation in archive.org scan of the 1929 Gollancz printing of Journey's End (in.ernet.dli.2015.209119), grepped verbatim contains no such offer.

findings.claim: “When Hardy says ‘Cheero’ while describing the previous company's devastating losses…” (L2 content, L6 content, L6 key fact, L6 practice Q6, L6 flashcard).
findings.truth: Hardy's “Cheero!” is his cheerful farewell after a chat about earwig racing, not a comment on casualties. His genuine understatement is earlier: “They simply blew us to bits yesterday… A dug-out got blown up and came down in the men's tea. They were frightfully annoyed.”
findings.evidence: archive.org scan of the 1929 Gollancz printing of Journey's End (in.ernet.dli.2015.209119), grepped verbatim, Act 1.

findings.claim: “AO3 (context) is worth up to 20 of the 40 content marks.”
findings.truth: The post-1914 play essay carries 40 marks in total: AO1 16 + AO3 16 + AO4 8 (spelling, punctuation and grammar). There are 32 content marks, not 40, and context is 16 of them.
findings.evidence: specs/edexcel/english-literature-1ET0.md — raw mark distribution table, questions 7–30 row (AO1 16, AO3 16, AO4 8, total 40); paper total 80, 1 hour 45 minutes, closed book.

findings.claim: Every essay mark scheme in all seven lessons uses the ladder “Top band (33–40+4 spelling/grammar) … Lower band (1–3+1 spelling/grammar)”, i.e. 40 content marks plus 4 for SPaG. Fourteen questions are typed “40 marks — Post-1914 Essay” but carry an 8-mark ladder (“Top band (7-8)”), and twelve are typed “4 marks — Quote Analysis”.
findings.truth: The 40+4 shape is AQA's 30+4 pattern rescaled; it is not Edexcel. The real split is 32 content marks + 8 SPaG marks = 40. Edexcel also sets no 4-mark or 8-mark question on this section — one essay only, from a choice of two, preceded by a short quotation. Options: (a) rebuild all 14 essay ladders on 32 + 8 and relabel the short questions as untimed study tasks rather than exam questions; or (b) hold this unit for the programme's existing 190 question-type relabels / 178 band-ladder queue so one house ladder lands everywhere at once. I recommend (b) — the band boundaries are a house decision, and 42 questions in one unit should not diverge from the rest of the corpus.
findings.evidence: specs/edexcel/english-literature-1ET0.md — Component overview and raw mark distribution.

findings.claim: Knowledge check 1 reads “Which assessment objectives are tested in Edexcel Component 1, Section B?”
findings.truth: “Component 1” is a banned spec code that fails the house validator for the whole unit. Question reworded to “the Edexcel post-1914 play question”. The answer key was already right: AO1, AO3 and AO4.
findings.evidence: CHECK_PROMPT banned-string list; spec confirms AO1/AO3/AO4 on this section.

findings.claim: “AO4 — spelling, punctuation, and grammar alongside accurate use of literary terminology”, and a flashcard “Which AO rewards spelling, punctuation, grammar and accurate terminology?” The same paragraph tells students to “check your exam board's specimen paper for the exact mark allocation”.
findings.truth: Subject terminology is credited under AO2, which is not assessed on this question at all. Edexcel AO4 is “use a range of vocabulary and sentence structures for clarity, purpose and effect, with accurate spelling and punctuation”. The mark allocation is known (32 + 8) and is now stated instead of deferred.
findings.evidence: specs/edexcel/english-literature-1ET0.md — Assessment Objectives and weightings.

findings.claim: Five sentences are broken mid-word or mid-clause, apparently by an earlier patch: L3 “will describe his censorship of his own letters was a real practice”; L3 “…them.” threatens to shoot Hibbert”; L5 “my best friend”” establishes the schoolboy bond”; L7 “what most cannot face.e play suggests”; L7 “as man to man,”t the Stanhope he finds”. A flashcard question also reads “Who is Stanhope's fiancée whom Raleigh's sister?”
findings.truth: Each has been restored to a sentence that parses, keeping every dfn, data-def and data-narration-id attribute and the same number of narration blocks.
findings.evidence: raw/L03.txt, raw/L05.txt, raw/L07.txt.

findings.claim: Two flashcard answers are the bare strings “AO3.” and “AO4.”
findings.truth: An AO code followed immediately by a full stop is rejected by the house validator as a spec-code pattern. Rewritten as “AO3 (context).” and “AO4 (spelling, punctuation and grammar).”
findings.evidence: CHECK_PROMPT validator limits.

findings.claim: “Madge Raleigh — Raleigh's older sister”, and Madge is called Stanhope's “fiancée” throughout the unit.
findings.truth: The play never gives Madge's age; Stanhope says he first thought of her as “another kid like Raleigh”. Raleigh says of Stanhope and Madge, “They're not — er — officially engaged”. The flashcard is corrected; the loose use of “fiancée” elsewhere is left alone as ordinary study-guide shorthand.
findings.evidence: archive.org scan of the 1929 Gollancz printing of Journey's End (in.ernet.dli.2015.209119), grepped verbatim, Act 1.

findings.claim: “Stanhope, Trotter, and Hibbert eat and drink while Osborne's empty chair sits at the table” (also a flashcard).
findings.truth: Sherriff's stage directions describe candles, two champagne bottles and the three men, but no empty chair. It is a reasonable directorial image, not a textual detail, and a student who cites it as evidence would be inventing.
findings.evidence: archive.org scan of the 1929 Gollancz printing of Journey's End (in.ernet.dli.2015.209119), grepped verbatim, Act 3 Scene 2 opening stage direction.

findings.claim: “Only Raleigh and a German prisoner return” from the raid (content and flashcard).
findings.truth: Stanhope reports “Four men and Raleigh came safely back”, and the Colonel asks after “the six men” who were lost with Osborne. Osborne and six men are killed; four men, Raleigh and one prisoner come back.
findings.evidence: archive.org scan of the 1929 Gollancz printing of Journey's End (in.ernet.dli.2015.209119), grepped verbatim, Act 3 Scene 1.

findings.claim: Mason “provides gentle comic relief through his complaints about the quality of food (‘a yellow sort of stuff, sir’)”.
findings.truth: Misquoted and mischaracterised. Osborne asks “What kind of soup is this, Mason?” and Mason answers, deadpan, “It's yellow soup, sir.” Mason apologises for the rations rather than complaining about them.
findings.evidence: archive.org scan of the 1929 Gollancz printing of Journey's End (in.ernet.dli.2015.209119), grepped verbatim, Act 1.

findings.claim: The phrase “Section B” appears nine times across the unit (L1, L3, L4, L5 ×2, L7 ×4).
findings.truth: The CHECK_PROMPT bans “Paper 1 Section B”-style codes. A bare “Section B” may or may not trip the house validator. “Component 1” has been removed; the remaining bare references are left in place. If the validator rejects them, they need one sweep to “the post-1914 play question” across all seven lessons.
findings.evidence: grep of raw/L0*.txt.

findings.claim: “By 1915 the Western Front had become a continuous line of trenches stretching from the English Channel to Switzerland.”
findings.truth: The line ran from the North Sea coast in Belgium to the Swiss border. “English Channel” is the common textbook loose form and would not cost a mark, so it is left alone.
findings.evidence: Standard WWI geography; no fix applied.

summary: Seven lessons, 24 findings (10 HIGH), 77 surgical edits. Three quotations are outright fabrications - “It's the only way to forget”, “It's just the light - it's nearly morning” and the Hibbert-scene line - and all three were on memorisation lists for a closed-book paper; two more real lines were given to the wrong speaker or act. Exam claims were AQA-shaped: the Edexcel post-1914 essay is 40 marks (AO1 16 + AO3 16 + AO4 8), not 40 content marks plus 4 SPaG, and every mark ladder in the unit still carries the wrong shape (F14, held for adjudication).
